title: Force and Motion
summary: A force is a push or a pull on an object. A force can make a body at rest move, change the speed of a moving body, change its direction of motion, or change its shape (pressing a balloon).

When equal forces act in opposite directions (two equal teams in a tug-of-war, or pushing a brick equally from both sides) they are balanced: the net force is zero and the state of rest or motion does not change, although balanced forces can change the shape of a body. When the forces are unequal they are unbalanced, and the body starts moving, speeds up, slows down or changes direction in the direction of the larger force.

Inertia is the tendency of a body to stay at rest or to keep moving with the same velocity — to resist any change in its state. Examples: a glass on a paper stays put when the paper is jerked away; dust leaves a carpet when it is beaten; leaves and fruits fall when a branch is shaken; sauce comes out when a bottle is jerked; a sprinter keeps running after the finish line. Mass is the measure of inertia — a full box or a cricket ball is harder to move or stop than an empty box or a table-tennis ball.

Newton's first law (law of inertia): every body continues in its state of rest or of uniform motion in a straight line unless it is compelled by an unbalanced force to change that state. When a bus starts suddenly, standing passengers fall backward (their feet move with the bus, the upper body stays at rest); when a moving bus stops suddenly they fall forward (the upper body keeps moving).

Momentum p = mass × velocity (p = mv); its SI unit is kg m s⁻¹ and it is a vector in the direction of velocity. A bullet fired from a gun or a moving truck has a large momentum and a large effect. Second law: the rate of change of momentum of a body is directly proportional to the force acting on it and takes place in the direction of the force. From F ∝ (mv − mu)/t we get F = ma. The SI unit of force is the newton (N): 1 N gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m s⁻² (about the weight of 100 g). Examples: a fielder moves his hands back while catching to increase the time and reduce the force; falling on a cement floor hurts but falling on sand does not; a karate player breaks tiles with a very fast blow; a string breaks when a bundle is jerked up.
## Newton's third law and conservation of momentum

Third law: to every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Action and reaction (i) are interchangeable, (ii) always act on two different bodies, so they do not cancel, and (iii) act at the same time; the bodies need not touch (two magnets). Examples: a released balloon moves opposite to the escaping air; a boat moves back when you jump ashore; we walk by pushing the ground back and the ground pushes us forward; a swimmer pushes water back; rockets and jet planes push hot gases backward; a gun recoils; a lawn sprinkler spins as water leaves it.

Law of conservation of momentum: when bodies collide or interact and no external force acts, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after (m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2). For a gun firing a bullet both start at rest, so 0 = MV + mv, giving the recoil velocity V = −mv/M (opposite to the bullet). Example: a 3 kg rifle firing a 0.03 kg bullet at 100 m/s recoils at 1 m/s.

Friction is the force that opposes motion between surfaces in contact; it is why a rolling ball or a car with its engine off slows down. Static friction acts before a body starts moving; sliding (kinetic) friction is slightly less; rolling friction is much less than sliding friction. Friction depends on the nature (smoothness) of the surfaces — a pencil cell rolls farthest on glass and least on sand — and on the normal reaction (a heavier box needs more force).

Advantages: we can walk, write, hold a nail in a wall, construct buildings; treaded tyres grip the road; brakes work. Disadvantages: energy is wasted as heat, machines wear out and become less efficient, shoe soles and steps wear away. Friction is reduced by lubricants (oil in a sewing machine), ball bearings (rolling instead of sliding) and smooth surfaces.

Thrust is the force acting perpendicular to a surface; pressure = thrust/area, with SI unit N m⁻² called the pascal (Pa), after Blaise Pascal. The same force on a smaller area gives more pressure: knives and axes have sharp edges and nails have pointed tips. To reduce pressure the area is increased: wide foundations of buildings and dams, wide tyres on heavy trucks, chains on army tanks, broad straps on school bags, a porter's round cloth pad, a camel's broad feet on sand.

objective: Read the passage and answer: 'In a game of tug-of-war, when the two teams pull the rope with equal force, the rope remains stationary. When one team applies greater force, it pulls the other team.' (a) What name is given to the forces on the rope when it does not move? (b) What type of force acts when one team pulls the rope towards itself?

Read the passage and answer: 'If the net external force on a body is zero, a body at rest remains at rest and a body in motion continues to move with uniform velocity. This property is called inertia.' (i) Name the quantity which causes the motion of a body initially at rest. (ii) While sitting in a moving bus, why do you feel a jerk when the bus suddenly stops?
(i) An (unbalanced) force. (ii) The lower part of the body stops with the bus, but the upper part keeps moving forward due to inertia of motion, so we are thrown forward.

Read the passage and answer: 'Newton's third law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. When we jump off the ground we push the ground down and the ground pushes us up. The action and reaction forces always occur in pairs and act on different objects.' (1) On which object does the reaction force act when you jump? (2) Why do action and reaction not cancel each other?
(1) On the person (the ground pushes the person upward). (2) Because they act on two different bodies.

case.passage: Momentum is the product of the mass and velocity of a body. According to Newton's second law, the rate of change of momentum is proportional to the applied force, which gives F = ma. When no external force acts on a system, its total momentum stays constant. So when a gun fires a bullet, the gun moves backward (recoils) so that the total momentum remains zero, as it was before firing.

vsa: Explain why a tailor oils his sewing machine regularly.

Friction between the moving parts of the machine causes wear and tear and wastes energy as heat. Oil (a lubricant) forms a thin layer between the parts and reduces friction, so the machine runs smoothly and lasts longer.
Why do passengers standing in a moving bus feel a forward jerk when the driver applies the brakes suddenly?
When the bus stops, the feet of the passengers stop with it, but the upper part of the body continues to move forward because of inertia of motion. So they lurch forward.
What is momentum? Give its SI unit.
Momentum is the product of the mass and velocity of a body, p = mv. Its SI unit is kg m s⁻¹, and it acts in the direction of the velocity (a vector).
Why does a boxer move his head backward while taking a punch?
Moving back increases the time in which the momentum of the punch becomes zero. A smaller rate of change of momentum means a smaller force, so the injury is reduced.
Why does a porter put a round piece of cloth on his head while carrying a heavy load?
The cloth increases the area over which the load acts. Since pressure = thrust/area, a larger area means less pressure on his head.
State two advantages and two disadvantages of friction.
Advantages: it lets us walk without slipping; it makes brakes work (also writing, holding nails). Disadvantages: it wastes energy as heat; it causes wear and tear of machine parts and shoe soles.
sa: A bullet of mass 20 g is fired horizontally from a gun of mass 5 kg with a velocity of 400 m/s. Calculate the recoil velocity of the gun.

By conservation of momentum, total momentum before = 0 = momentum after. m = 0.02 kg, v = 400 m/s, M = 5 kg. 0 = MV + mv ⇒ V = −mv/M = −(0.02 × 400)/5 = −1.6 m/s. The gun recoils with 1.6 m/s, opposite to the bullet.

A constant force acting on a body of mass 4.0 kg changes its speed from 1.0 m/s to 2.5 m/s in 25 s, the direction of motion remaining unchanged. What are the magnitude and direction of the force?
a = (v − u)/t = (2.5 − 1.0)/25 = 0.06 m/s². F = ma = 4.0 × 0.06 = 0.24 N, acting in the direction of motion.
April 2025
A hammer of mass 400 g moving at 40 m/s strikes a nail. The nail stops the hammer in 0.01 s. What is the force of the nail on the hammer?
m = 0.4 kg, u = 40 m/s, v = 0, t = 0.01 s. F = m(v − u)/t = 0.4 × (0 − 40)/0.01 = −1600 N. The nail exerts a force of 1600 N on the hammer, opposite to its motion.
October 2024
State Newton's second law of motion. Using it, derive the unit of force. A person pushes a box of mass 50 kg with a force of 80 N. Calculate the acceleration.

The rate of change of momentum of a body is proportional to the force acting on it and is in the direction of the force; this gives F = ma. Unit: F = 1 kg × 1 m s⁻² = 1 kg m s⁻² = 1 newton. a = F/m = 80/50 = 1.6 m/s².
April 2017
What is meant by momentum? Give its SI unit. Is it scalar or vector? A force of 68 N produces an acceleration of 1.7 m/s² in a body. Find its mass.
Momentum = mass × velocity; SI unit kg m s⁻¹; it is a vector (direction of velocity). m = F/a = 68/1.7 = 40 kg.
October 2017
State three significant features of Newton's third law of motion. How does it explain walking on the earth?

(1) Action and reaction are equal and opposite and interchangeable. (2) They act on two different bodies. (3) They act simultaneously. While walking we push the ground backward with our foot (action); the ground pushes our foot forward with an equal force (reaction), and this reaction moves us forward.

sa: (a) Can a body moving with constant speed still have acceleration? Explain with an example. (b) Can action and reaction act on the same body? Give reason.

(a) Yes. If its direction changes, its velocity changes, so it accelerates — e.g. a body moving at constant speed in a circle (a merry-go-round). (b) No. Action and reaction always act on two different bodies; if they acted on the same body they would cancel and no motion would result.
October 2022
la: What is inertia? Describe an activity to show the property of inertia. Why do passengers standing in a bus fall backward when a stationary bus starts suddenly?

Inertia is the tendency of a body to remain at rest or in uniform motion and resist any change in its state; mass measures it. Activity: place a glass half filled with water on a strip of paper at the edge of a table and pull the paper out with a quick jerk — the glass stays where it is, because of its inertia of rest. When a bus starts suddenly, the feet of standing passengers move forward with the bus, but the upper part of their body tends to stay at rest due to inertia, so they fall backward.
What is the force of friction? Describe an activity to show that friction depends on the smoothness of the surfaces. Write two advantages and two disadvantages of friction.

Friction is the force that opposes the relative motion of two surfaces in contact. Activity: set up an inclined plane on a table and release a pencil cell from a marked line; note how far it rolls on the bare table, on a glass sheet and on a layer of sand. It goes farthest on glass and least on sand, showing that smoother surfaces have less friction (friction also depends on the normal reaction). Advantages: walking without slipping; brakes and tyre grip. Disadvantages: wastage of energy as heat; wear and tear of machine parts.
